result_text:
TRACK 2 — Bootstrap, module loading & core site engine
Files reviewed: assets/js/script.js (854 ln), assets/js/modules/core.js (784 ln). Repo HEAD at review time: 04f3c36 (matches task context).

## 1. The 29 INFERRED bootSite() edges — VERIFIED CORRECT

script.js:770-803 `bootSite()` contains exactly 33 lines of the form `if (typeof X === 'function') X();` (confirmed by direct count — matches the god-node's "33 edges" 1:1, one edge per guarded call, including the final `loadGA4` which is registered via `addEventListener('load', loadGA4)` rather than called directly).

`initAccessControl` (script.js:789) is defined at access.js:859. `initAudioCues` (script.js:800) is defined at audio.js:128. Both are real, direct, unconditional call sites in bootSite() — the graph's inferred relationship is factually correct, not a hallucinated/spurious edge.

Why graphify marked these 29 as INFERRED rather than EXTRACTED: none of the 8 modules use ES `import`/`export` or an IIFE-scoped namespace — every module (core.js, tour.js, cmdk.js, ui.js, access.js, audio.js, terminal.js, haptics.js) declares its functions as bare global `function` statements (verified via grep across all 8 files). script.js has no static reference to which file defines `initAccessControl` — it only knows the symbol name and hopes it exists on `window` after the dynamic loader resolves. A pure AST/import-graph extractor genuinely cannot resolve this cross-file link without name-matching inference, so "INFERRED" is the right classification for graphify to have made — not a graph defect.

**Verdict: all 29 inferred edges from bootSite() to cross-module functions are real and correct.** Recommend the graph maintainers mark this community's inferred edges as human-verified in the next `graphify update`.

## 2. Module-loader failure-mode analysis (script.js:8-34)

Loader creates 8 `<script>` tags with `async=false` (preserves execution order) and both `onload`/`onerror` calling `resolve()` on each per-module promise — i.e. `Promise.all(promises)` can never reject, so one failed module never blocks the others from initializing. This graceful-degradation intent is good, but has three concrete gaps:

**[HIGH] No timeout — a stalled (not failed) request hangs the entire boot forever.**
script.js:8-34. `onerror` only fires on an actual network/HTTP failure. If a request merely stalls (flaky connection, captive portal, browser deprioritizing a background tab) it never fires `load` or `error`, so that module's promise never settles, `Promise.all` never resolves, and `bootSite()` — nav, footer, theme, access control, everything — never runs. This is a strictly worse outcome than a clean 404 (which degrades gracefully via the `typeof` guards). Fix: wrap each module promise in a `Promise.race([modulePromise, timeoutPromise(Nms)])` so a stalled module degrades like a failed one instead of blocking boot indefinitely.

**[HIGH] `healthcheck`'s module-loaded check is a false positive by construction.**
terminal.js:130-136. It checks `document.querySelectorAll('script[src*="modules/"]')` against the expected filename list. But `document.head.appendChild(s)` (script.js:29) runs unconditionally and synchronously for all 8 modules before any network request resolves — the `<script>` tag is *always* present in the DOM whether the load succeeded, 404'd, or is still stalled. This check can never actually detect a missing/failed module; it will report "✓ Modules: all 8 loaded" even when several silently failed. This is the one diagnostic tool the v45 changelog (script.js:60) explicitly says exists to catch module-loading problems, and it cannot do so. Fix: check `typeof <oneCanaryFnPerModule> === 'function'` (e.g. `initTheme`, `initTour`, `renderCmdk`, `initAudioCues`, `initAccessControl`, etc.) instead of DOM tag presence, or have the loader set `window.__moduleLoadStatus[src] = 'ok'|'error'` in the actual load/error handlers and read that.

**[MEDIUM] No error surfacing anywhere in the boot path** — confirmed via grep: only two `console.error` calls exist in the entire codebase (access.js:77 payload-decryption, access.js:183 JWT-parse), neither related to module loading. There is no `window.onerror`, no `addEventListener('error', ...)` on the script tags beyond the silent `resolve()`, and no telemetry. Combined with finding #2, a failed/stalled `core.js` load is completely invisible — it doesn't break anything loudly, it just silently degrades. This surfaces downstream, non-obviously: e.g. `handleGoogleCredentialResponse()` (access.js:229-250) references `SITE.masterEmails`/`SITE.vipEmails` (access.js:240-243) with **no `typeof` guard**, unlike haptics.js:146 which does guard (`typeof SITE === 'undefined'`). If core.js (which defines `SITE`) fails to load, a user attempting Google Sign-In gets an uncaught `ReferenceError` deep in an OAuth callback with zero trail back to "core.js failed to load" — this would present to the site owner as "sign-in doesn't work" with no diagnostic path. Fix: at minimum, guard access.js:240-243 the same way haptics.js does; ideally log module-load failures to `console.error` /a visible toast so `initServiceWorker`-style silent degradation doesn't extend to auth-critical paths.

**[LOW/nit] Not all initialization is actually centralized through bootSite().** ui.js has two top-level IIFEs (`initCursorTrail` ~ui.js:456, `initMasterEscapeHandler` ~ui.js:496) and terminal.js has its own self-invoking `setup()` gate (terminal.js:288-293) that run independent of `window.__modulesLoadedPromise`/`bootSite()` — they self-initialize on their own module's parse (immediately if `document.readyState !== 'loading'`, else on `DOMContentLoaded`). Functionally fine today (their internal calls into other modules are all deferred inside event listeners with their own `typeof` guards), but it means "bootSite is the boot orchestrator" is not literally true — there are 3 independent init entry points outside the 33-edge god node. Worth a comment/README note for future contributors, not a bug.

## 3. Community 0 (cohesion 0.05) — is it a real code smell?

**No — recommend not treating this as an actionable split.** Community 0's 53 nodes are, per source inspection, essentially "everything declared at top level in script.js (6 items: `SITE_RELEASES`, `SEARCH_STATIC_INDEX`, `bootSite`, `initServiceWorker`, `initReadingProgressBar`, `initNetworkStatusListeners`) + everything in core.js (~34 items: nav/footer rendering, theme, accent, hamburger, scroll, reveal, cursor, GA4, and the full Bikram Sambat calendar subsystem)." Low cohesion here is the expected, inherent signature of a hub node (`bootSite`, 33 edges — the single highest-fan-out node in the whole 411-node graph) pulled into one community with its neighbors by modularity-based clustering: hub-and-spoke stars trivially produce near-zero intra-community edge density because almost all edges are hub→leaf, not leaf→leaf, regardless of whether the leaves are actually related to each other. `SEARCH_STATIC_INDEX` (search data) and `adToBs()` (Bikram Sambat date conversion) have no real relationship to each other; they're grouped only because both are reachable from `bootSite`/live in the same two files. The runtime code is *already* decomposed by concern into 8 module files (core/tour/cmdk/ui/access/audio/terminal/haptics) — that decomposition happened at the v42 refactor per the changelog (script.js:95). Splitting "Community 0" isn't a code change with a clear boundary; it's a graph-clustering artifact.

**One genuine, concrete, low-severity extraction is worth calling out, though:** the Bikram Sambat calendar utility inside core.js — `BS_YEARS`/`BS_MONTHS`/`BS_EPOCH_UTC`/`AD_MONTHS` (core.js:724-727), `kathmanduYMD()` (730), `adToBs()` (738), `computeLiveDates()`/`applyLiveDates()` (632, 707), `renderStatusDate()`/`toggleStatusDate()`/`initStatusDate()` (754-768) — is a fully self-contained ~10-node subsystem with no dependency on the rest of core.js (nav/theme/footer) beyond being called from `bootSite`. Unlike "split Community 0" (no real file boundary), extracting this into its own `assets/js/modules/date.js` (9th module, loaded like the others) is a concrete, low-risk refactor that would measurably raise core.js's own internal cohesion. Flagging as low/nit — not urgent, but the one legitimately actionable idea to come out of the cohesion question.
